analysis.one_liner: Designates 1.56 million acres of the Arctic Refuge coastal plain as protected wilderness, off-limits to oil drilling.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past its committee referral and died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021, leaving the coastal plain open to oil leasing.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have permanently protected the coastal plain of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge in Alaska as wilderness, a designation that bars roads, development, and oil drilling on about 1,559,538 acres [S2][S3]. This matters because Congress opened that same area to oil leasing in the 2017 tax law; wilderness designation would have reversed that. The bill was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before Congress ended [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Members of the public who value the refuge — including Alaska Native communities like the Gwich'in whose way of life is tied to the caribou herd that calves on the coastal plain — gain permanent protection of the area. Future generations get a preserved wilderness rather than an industrial oil field.
analysis.who_benefits_short: The public and Alaska Native communities

how_it_helps.text: Designates approximately 1,559,538 acres of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge coastal plain as wilderness under the Wilderness Act, permanently barring development and roads there [S2][S3].

Wilderness designation would override the 2017 provision that opened the coastal plain to oil leasing, keeping the calving grounds of the Porcupine caribou herd and habitat for polar bears and migratory birds undisturbed — an explanation of how the Wilderness Act works, not a claim from the record.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies lose access to a potential drilling frontier, and Alaska's state government loses anticipated revenue and jobs it projected from coastal plain development (state projections are general context, not from the record).

drawbacks.text: The United States forgoes development of an oil field the federal government estimated could hold billions of barrels of technically recoverable oil; supporters of drilling argue domestic production lowers energy costs and reduces reliance on foreign oil (general policy context, not from the record).

Alaska Natives of the Inupiat village of Kaktovik, located on the coastal plain, have supported development because of the jobs and revenue it could bring — a long-standing split within Alaska Native communities (widely reported, not from the record).
The bill designates wilderness by legislative map reference without any new study or process, which opponents called an end-run around the normal land-management review process (general context).

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill traded a large but speculative industrial and fiscal benefit for permanent protection of the largest remaining intact Arctic ecosystem in the United States. The cost falls on a concentrated set of drillers and the state of Alaska; the benefit is diffuse and long-term, which is why wilderness bills rarely move unless they are part of a large land package.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Environment and Public Works Committee the day it was introduced, never got a hearing or vote, and died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Markey and five other Democratic senators introduced the bill on September 11, 2019 [S3][S5].
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works that same day — its only action [S5].
No hearing, markup, or floor vote ever occurred before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S1][S5].
Meanwhile, the first oil lease sale on the coastal plain under the 2017 law was scheduled for January 2021, so the area remained on track for development (widely reported context).

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies and the Alaska state government are better off, because the coastal plain stayed open to leasing; nothing now prevents drilling there.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil drillers and the state of Alaska

for.name: Chuck Schumer

sides.party_line_note: All 34 supporters were Democrats or the Independent; no Republicans cosponsored, and Republicans controlled the Senate committee and floor schedule.

industries.note: The bill would have permanently barred drilling on the coastal plain, which Congress had opened to leasing in 2017. Because the bill died, drillers keep access to the area and the public bears the environmental risk instead.

industries.industry: Alaska state government and Alaska Native corporations with development stakes
industries.note: The state loses projected revenue and jobs the bill would have foreclosed, but wilderness protection preserves the caribou herds that the Gwich'in people depend on. The bill died, so the state keeps the option of drilling revenue.
